lessons.subject: chemistry
lessons.title: States of matter

slides.title: What is matter?
slides.oldHtml:
What is matter?

Anything that has mass and volume
Mass: the amount of matter (kg)
Volume: the space it takes up (m3 or L)
Three main states: solid, liquid, gas
slides.newHtml:
What is matter?

Anything that has mass and volume
Mass: the amount of matter (kg)
Volume: the space it takes up (m3 or L)
Solid
Liquid
Gas

slides.title: Solids
slides.oldHtml:
Solids

Fixed positions in a regular lattice
Vibrate, more when heated
Fixed shape and volume
High density
Strong forces of attraction
slides.newHtml:
Solids

  • Fixed positions in a regular lattice
  • Vibrate about fixed positions (more when heated)
  • Fixed shape and fixed volume
  • High density — cannot be compressed
Forces of attraction: Strong

slides.title: Liquids
slides.oldHtml:
Liquids

Close together (touching), random
Move past each other
Fixed volume, takes the container's shape
Can't be compressed easily
Weak forces of attraction
slides.newHtml:
Liquids

  • Close together (touching), random arrangement
  • Move past each other (faster when heated)
  • Fixed volume, takes the shape of the container
  • Cannot be compressed easily
Forces of attraction: Weak

slides.title: Gases
slides.oldHtml:
Gases

Random and far apart
Move freely, faster when heated
Fill any container
Low density, easily compressed
Very weak forces of attraction
slides.newHtml:
Gases

  • Random and far apart
  • Move freely in all directions (faster when heated)
  • No fixed shape or volume — fill any container
  • Low density — easily compressed
Forces of attraction: Very weak

slides.title: Changes of state
slides.oldHtml:
Changes of state

Caused by changes in temperature and/or pressure, which change the particles' kinetic energy
They are reversible
Also called interconversions or transitions
slides.newHtml:
Changes of state

Caused by changes in temperature and/or pressure
  • Change the particles' kinetic energy
  • They are reversible physical changes
  • Also called interconversions or transitions
Dry ice (solid CO₂) sublimating into gas

slides.title: Melting and freezing
slides.oldHtml:
Melting and freezing

Heating: particles vibrate more
At the melting point they break free and move around: melting
Cooling: at the freezing point they are held in place again
melting point = freezing point
slides.newHtml:
Melting and freezing

  • Heating a solid: particles vibrate more
  • At the melting point they overcome fixed positions and move around: melting
  • Cooling a liquid: at the freezing point forces hold them in place again
melting point = freezing point

slides.title: Boiling and condensing
slides.oldHtml:
Boiling and condensing

Heating a liquid: particles move faster
At the boiling point they overcome all the forces of attraction
→ spread far apart: boiling
Condensing is the opposite, caused by cooling
slides.newHtml:
Boiling and condensing

  • Heating a liquid: particles move faster
  • At the boiling point they overcome all forces of attraction
  • Particles spread far apart → boiling
Condensing: gas → liquid when cooled

slides.title: Evaporation
slides.oldHtml:
Evaporation

Liquid → gas without boiling
Particles at the surface gain enough energy to escape
Faster at higher temperature or in direct sunlight
slides.newHtml:
Evaporation

Liquid → gas without boiling
  • Fastest particles at the surface escape into the air
  • Happens at any temperature below the boiling point
  • Faster at higher temperature, wind, or wider surface
Boiling forms gas bubbles throughout the whole liquid at the boiling point.

slides.title: Temperature and state
slides.oldHtml:
Temperature and state

Water: melts at 0 °C, boils at 100 °C
What state is water at 24 °C?
→ liquid (it's between 0 and 100)
At exactly 0 °C or 100 °C it could be in either state
slides.newHtml:
Temperature and state

Water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C
What state is water at 24 °C?
→ Liquid (24 °C is between 0 °C and 100 °C)
  • At exactly 0 °C or 100 °C, it can be in either state
  • Compare the given temperature to the melting and boiling points

slides.title: Which has stronger forces?
slides.oldHtml:
Which has stronger forces?

Air or olive oil?
Air is a gas at room temperature: its boiling point is below it (about −195 °C)
Olive oil is a liquid: its boiling point is above room temperature
Stronger forces → more energy to separate the particles → higher boiling point
slides.newHtml:
Which has stronger forces?

Air or olive oil?
  • Air is a gas at room temperature (boils at about −195 °C)
  • Olive oil is a liquid at room temperature (boiling point well above 25 °C)
Stronger forces → more energy needed to separate particles → higher boiling point

slides.title: Why is the graph flat?
slides.newHtml:
Why is the graph flat?

We are still heating the ice, so why does the temperature stay flat at 0 °C?
AHeat energy stops entering the ice
BEnergy is used to overcome forces of attraction between particles
CParticles stop vibrating while melting
⚠ EXAMINER TIP: Flat plateau = change of state — energy overcomes attractions, NOT raising temperature!

slides.title: Particles are fast!
slides.oldHtml:
Particles are fast!

Gas particles move at hundreds of m/s (hydrogen ≈ 1700 m/s)
So why is diffusion slow?
They keep colliding and changing direction
Higher temperature → faster particles → faster diffusion
slides.newHtml:
Particles are fast!

Gas particles travel at hundreds of m/s (hydrogen ≈ 1700 m/s)
So why is diffusion slow?
  • Particles constantly collide and change direction
  • Higher temperature → faster particles → faster diffusion

slides.title: Ammonia + hydrogen chloride
slides.oldHtml:
Ammonia + hydrogen chloride

They react → white ring of ammonium chloride
Nearer the HCl end: NH3 is lighter, so it moves faster
slides.newHtml:
Ammonia + hydrogen chloride

Where they meet, they react → white ring of ammonium chloride
Closer to HCl end: NH3 is lighter, so it moves faster

slides.title: Dilution
slides.oldHtml:
Dilution

Less purple each time: fewer KMnO4 particles per water particle
Still purple after many dilutions → particles are very small and very many
slides.newHtml:
Dilution

  • Less purple each time — fewer KMnO4 particles per water particle
  • Still faintly purple after many dilutions → particles are very small and very many

slides.title: Key words (1 of 2)
slides.oldHtml:
Key words (1 of 2)

Solution: the mixture formed when a substance dissolves
Solute: the substance that dissolves (e.g. salt)
Solvent: the liquid it dissolves in (usually water)
slides.newHtml:
Key words (1 of 2)

Solution: the mixture formed when a substance dissolves
Solute: the substance that dissolves (e.g. salt)
Solvent: the liquid it dissolves in (usually water)

slides.title: Key words (2 of 2)
slides.oldHtml:
Key words (2 of 2)

Dissolve: a soluble substance mixing completely into a liquid
Soluble / insoluble: can / cannot dissolve
Saturated: no more solute can dissolve
slides.newHtml:
Key words (2 of 2)

Dissolve: a soluble substance mixing completely into a liquid
Soluble / insoluble: can / cannot dissolve
Saturated: no more solute can dissolve

slides.title: Is sugar water pure?
slides.oldHtml:
Is sugar water pure?

No! Pure = only one substance. A solution is a mixture (separable by physical processes)
slides.newHtml:
Is sugar water pure?

No! Pure = only one substance. A solution is a mixture (separable by physical processes).

slides.title: Saturated
slides.oldHtml:
Saturated

No more solute can dissolve
Different solvents have different saturation points
At 20 °C, 1 litre of water dissolves about 357 g of salt
slides.newHtml:
Saturated

No more solute can dissolve
  • Different solvents have different saturation points
  • At 20 °C, 1 litre of water dissolves about 357 g of salt
  • Extra solid settles at the bottom as undissolved crystals

slides.title: Sodium → sodium ion
slides.oldHtml:
Sodium → sodium ion

Na   2.8.1  →  loses 1 electron → Na+   2.8
11 protons (+), 10 electrons (−) → overall 1+ · no need to draw the empty outer shell
slides.newHtml:
Sodium → sodium ion

Na   2.8.1  →  loses 1 electron → Na+   2.8
11 protons (+), 10 electrons (−) → overall 1+  |  no need to draw the empty outer shell

slides.title: Molecules can be ions too
slides.oldHtml:
Molecules can be ions too

Hydroxide, OH−: an oxygen atom joined to a hydrogen atom
The group has gained one extra electron
→ charge of 1−
also NO3− · CO32− · SO42− · NH4+
slides.newHtml:
Molecules can be ions too

Hydroxide, OH−: an oxygen atom joined to a hydrogen atom
The group has gained one extra electron
→ charge of 1−
also: NO3−,  CO32−,  SO42−,  NH4+

slides.title: Electron transfer
slides.oldHtml:
Electron transfer

The metal (Na) loses an electron → cation Na+ · the non-metal (F) gains it → anion F−
slides.newHtml:
Electron transfer

The metal (Na) loses an electron → cation Na+  |  the non-metal (F) gains it → anion F−

slides.title: Dot & cross: sodium chloride
slides.oldHtml:
Dot & cross: sodium chloride

Brackets + charges · anion has 8 · no shell needed for the metal ion
slides.newHtml:
Dot & cross: sodium chloride

Brackets + charges  |  anion has 8 outer electrons  |  no shell needed for the metal ion

slides.title: Solid vs molten NaCl
slides.newHtml:
Solid vs molten NaCl

Why does molten NaCl conduct, while solid NaCl does not?
ASolid NaCl has no electrons to carry charge
BWhen molten, the ions are free to move and carry charge
CMelting turns the ions into covalent molecules
⚠ EXAMINER TRAP: NEVER say "electrons move" in ionic compounds — it is IONS that move!
